strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful way to build approximate four-point three-view pose hypotheses from established five-point and P3P solvers. This provides an accessible alternative to substantially more complicated algebraic and learned homotopy methods.

The empirical support is substantial: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, evaluation in PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, and supplementary experiments covering noise, geometry, outliers, and threshold sensitivity. The alternative metric incorporating all three camera pairs strengthens the evaluation.

The practical benefits persist against an enhanced baseline. In Table 3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves essentially the same PhotoTourism AUC@10 as 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM (76.16 versus 76.20) at lower runtime (44.51 versus 56.52 ms), with similar benefits on Cambridge and Aachen.

The ablations demonstrate why refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting matter. Hyperparameters are validated on a held-out scene, and the manuscript provides code and archived data links. The algorithmic simplicity and implementation details give a credible basis for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claim of consistently best speed–accuracy trade-offs is stronger than the comparisons establish. Figure 4 omits the enhanced five-point baseline with +R+F, although Tables 2–3 show these additions substantially improve it. Against the fully enhanced baseline, the most accurate proposed variant gains only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 AUC@10 percentage points across the three datasets while taking approximately 1.7–2.0 times longer. The tables support useful operating points, but the missing matched-baseline curves limit claims of general dominance.

The HC timing protocol complicates the efficiency comparison. Section 8.3 reports approximately 45 ms for loading network data once per RANSAC run, compared with total HC runtimes of roughly 60–67 ms in Table 3. Reporting timings with these reusable data already resident would clarify how much of the claimed speed advantage comes from solver computation.

The geometric bound provides limited assurance about pose accuracy. Lemma 1 bounds the synthetic correspondence's epipolar distance by the triangle's spatial extent, which can be large; it does not bound pose error or establish convergence of refinement. Figure 9 also shows residual errors on noiseless inputs. The practical contribution is well supported empirically, but the assertion that ENM makes scene dependence negligible is insufficiently qualified.

There are correctable mathematical and reporting issues. The sentence following Lemma 1 states equality with the maximum centroid-to-vertex distance, whereas the argument establishes an upper bound. In Table 7, the Cambridge results for the M+R+F and M+R+F+ENM variants exactly repeat the corresponding affine variants across all reported quantities, warranting verification.
